description:
We are a team from Tajikistan passionate about technology, Earth science, and turning complex data into useful products.

Our skills include iOS development (Swift, SwiftUI, MapKit), GIS, spatial data analysis, and data visualization.

We enjoy building real-world solutions using NASA open data.

We're looking for motivated teammates with experience in Python, data science, meteorology, remote sensing, GIS, or UI/UX design who want to create something impactful together!
summary:
Lunar Horizon is a public web tool that helps answer two key questions for landers near the Moon's south pole: when will sunlight be available for power, and when will Earth be visible for direct communication?

Choose a landing site and touchdown time to see the Sun and Earth against the local terrain horizon, hour by hour, throughout the mission.

If the launch is delayed, a site-by-date calendar helps explore alternatives. It provides two recommendations: the best landing day at the selected site and the best site for the selected day.

Near the lunar south pole, the Sun stays just a few degrees above the horizon, so nearby ridges can block sunlight for hours or even days. A change of just one day can turn zero hours of continuous Sun and Earth visibility into almost two weeks.

The tool uses terrain data from NASA LRO LOLA and Sun and Earth positions from JPL DE421. All 12 comparisons with JPL Horizons agree within 0.006°.

No installation or login required.
details:
What it does

Lunar Horizon shows what the sky looks like from a lunar landing site throughout a surface mission.

Users can select a landing site, date, touchdown time (UTC) and mission duration (from 1 to 30 days). The sky view shows the Sun and Earth against the local terrain horizon, at their apparent angular sizes. It also shows their paths throughout the mission and the illuminated phase of Earth. For sites south of 75°S, the horizon is based on real terrain data from NASA LRO LOLA.

Users can play the mission timeline and explore how the sky changes over time.

The information panels show the Sun's and Earth's elevation and azimuth, the percentage of the solar disc above the horizon, and the time until the next rise or set. A mission summary shows the longest continuous period with both the Sun and Earth visible from touchdown, the total percentage of the mission with both visible, the longest period without sunlight and the longest period without Earth visibility.

If the launch is delayed, a site-by-date calendar helps compare alternative landing opportunities. It uses colour to show how long both the Sun and Earth remain continuously above the local terrain horizon from touchdown. Two recommendations help users find the best landing day at the selected site within ±14 days and the best site for the selected day. A week-by-week view covers the period through December 2030.

The 3D view shows a 38 × 38 km area of lunar terrain around each polar site, with lighting based on the Sun's position at the selected time. Users can also add their own coordinates anywhere on the Moon and share a selected scenario through a link.

For example, at the IM-2 landing site, a 14-day mission starting on 15 December 2026 at 00:00 UTC has zero hours of continuous Sun and Earth visibility from touchdown. Landing just one day later gives 13 days and 15 hours.

How it works

1. Sun and Earth positions: We use the JPL DE421 ephemeris to calculate the positions of the Sun and Earth every three hours, from 15 November 2026 to 31 December 2030, in the Moon's mean-Earth reference frame. The page then computes where they appear in the sky for an observer 2 metres above the ground.

2. Terrain analysis: For each of the seven study points south of 75°S, a Python script processes the NASA LRO LOLA LDEM_75S_240M elevation model. It calculates the local horizon in 1,440 directions, with a 0.25° step, taking the Moon's curvature into account.

3. Visibility calculations: The Sun is considered visible when the centre of its disc is above the terrain horizon. Earth is counted as usable for a direct link when its centre is at least 2° above the horizon. Users can also choose a threshold of 0° or 5°.

4. Validation: We compared our Sun and Earth directions with JPL Horizons at two sites across six dates. All 12 comparisons agree within 0.006°, well inside our 0.02° tolerance. We also developed seven automated tests for the terrain calculations, map projection and orientation, and known terrain features such as Shackleton crater.

Benefits and intended impact

Lunar Horizon helps mission planners explore how the choice of landing site and touchdown time affects sunlight availability and visibility of Earth. It also helps them compare alternatives when a launch is delayed.

By bringing terrain, astronomical positions and mission timelines together in one interface, the tool makes complex information easier to explore and understand.

It can also be used for educational purposes and public exploration of lunar landing conditions. The tool works in any modern browser, on a phone or laptop, with no installation or login required.

What makes it creative

Lunar Horizon brings several types of information together on one page: real lunar terrain, the positions of the Sun and Earth, and landing dates.

Its site-by-date calendar turns a launch delay into a visual comparison of alternative landing opportunities. Instead of checking each site and date separately, users can compare them in one view and receive two recommendations.

The combination of a realistic terrain horizon, Earth's illuminated phase, a 3D terrain view and a mission timeline makes it possible to explore landing conditions from different perspectives.

We also compare our astronomical calculations with JPL Horizons to check their accuracy.

Factors considered and limitations

Each landing site is represented by a single point, not an entire landing region. Even a location a few hundred metres away can have a different horizon, especially near ridges.

The LOLA terrain model has a resolution of 240 metres and cannot resolve ridges smaller than approximately 500 metres. As a result, calculated rise and set times may differ from actual conditions by several hours.

Sites north of 75°S and user-added points use a smooth Moon model without detailed local terrain.

The 3D view shows only the 38 × 38 km area around the site; the visibility figures use the full terrain horizon out to the edge of the LOLA map.

The tool calculates geometric line of sight only. It does not account for ground stations, relay satellites, terrain slopes or thermal constraints. Therefore, visibility of Earth does not guarantee an actual communication link, and sunlight visibility does not guarantee power generation.

Positions are computed every 3 hours; rise and set times between samples are interpolated.

Lunar Horizon is an exploration and planning support tool, not a flight-certified mission-planning system.

Tools and technologies

- Frontend: HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with no build step.

- 3D visualization: three.js.

- Data processing: Python 3, NumPy, jplephem and DE421.

- Data sources: NASA LRO LOLA, JPL DE421 and JPL Horizons.

- Hosting: GitHub Pages.

Source code: https://github.com/Mehrafruz/lunar-horizon (MIT License).
